strengths: It designs a Visual Grounding task more closely aligned with real-world applications.

The paper provides a detailed discussion of the process for generating the SG3D dataset, including the specifics of how prompts are designed to generate tasks and the measures taken to minimize potential biases during the generation process.
The paper provides the basic experimental results on the new benchmark and implements several baselines from different paradigms, and a human study further validates the benchmark's validity.

The authors created a large-scale SG3D visual grounding benchmark based on adding additional automated text markup to 3D scenes from well-known datasets ScanNet, ARKitScenes, 3RScan, MultiScan, HM3D. Such a dataset is useful for planning actions by an intelligent agent on static scenes.

The authors clearly demonstrated the advantages of the task-oriented steps in SG3D and object-centric referrals they created, including using the example of markup from ScanRefer for the same target objects.

The paper proposes the sequential grounding task and a new dataset for this task. Compared to existing visual grounding tasks, sequential grounding needs the agent to incorporate more environmental and instructional context. This is more challenging in terms of 3D visual grounding.
The paper provides a detailed analysis of the introduced dataset.

This paper evaluates several existing 3D vision-language model baselines on the proposed task. The results show that these models only show limited performance, and there is a research gap to be filled. Ablation studies also show the importance of contextual information and the effect of the amount of training data.
This paper is well-written and easy to follow.
The SG3D dataset is built on a diverse foundation, incorporating 4,895 3D scenes spanning five distinct categories, resulting in a robust and varied dataset.
The task-centered design of textual instructions, focused on guiding sequential actions rather than mere object identification, is particularly valuable.
weaknesses: The benchmark does not fundamentally differ from traditional Visual Grounding benchmarks and the authors have not justified what new significant challenges this benchmark brings, questioning the fundamental value of the benchmark.

The introduction and abstract note the usefulness of the created dataset for intelligent agents and robots, but the task examples shown in Figure 1 look strange for a robot agent and may be more suitable for NPC characters in computer games; the authors do not mention this and should adjust the introduction to more accurately explain the motivation.

The authors use only three models (3D-VisTA, PQ3D, and LEO) to demonstrate the quality of modern methods on the created dataset, without sufficient justification for this limited selection, and omit other existing models, raising questions about the completeness and sufficiency of the results.
The article lacks an ablation study for the selected modifications of the 3D-VisTA, PQ3D, and LEO models, which would add validity to the results obtained.

The benchmark considers only the combination of pre-trained GPT-4 (with closed code) and a 3D object classifier, and it would be interesting to see experiments with other open-source models to enhance reproducibility.

The definition of the sequential grounding task is limited; it only links each step to a 3D object and omits important factors such as action decomposition, pre- and post-conditions, object verification, recovery from missing objects, and tool usage, making the task and dataset limited for real-world task planning.
It is unclear what embodiment (agent) is intended for the proposed dataset; many tasks/steps appear designed for humans rather than robots, raising doubts about usefulness for AI task planning.
The paper does not propose a novel method (a stronger baseline) for the proposed task.
Images in Figure 9 Task 1 are too blurry, making it impossible to assess whether predictions are reasonable.

The experimental evaluation is unclear, making it difficult to discern whether the model outputs bounding boxes or target IDs; supplementary material lacks corresponding label data and the origin of bounding boxes in Figure 9 remains unexplained.

The proposed method outputs only target-specific information at each step without addressing movement between steps, raising questions about continuity and whether the scene input is the same for each step, which would contradict perspective shifts in real-world applications.

The dataset's purpose seems limited and misaligned, focusing on grounding tasks where multiple steps appear unnecessary and confusing, and without a memory mechanism, ensuring consistency across steps is unconvincing.

The claim that the task requires understanding each step in the context of the whole plan is not adequately supported by the dataset design or experimental setup, as models are not explicitly evaluated on their ability to leverage such contextual information.
